payload.name: Past visits only when enumerating visited places
payload.description: Use when a question asks which places a person has been to, visited, or traveled to; require past completed presence and exclude plans or aspirational mentions.
content: When a question asks for locations a person 'has been to' or 'visited', list only memories that document a completed past physical presence (event with past timestamp or past-tense activity). Exclude plan memories, future-dated intentions, and aspirational statements even if the person is excited or has added them to a travel list.

Do not infer presence from reading about a place, joining a travel-related group, or discussing a place; require an explicit activity at the location (e.g., visited, toured, took a photo in, hiked in).
Before finalizing, run at least one additional search combining the person's name with activity terms that imply presence (photo, trip, visited, went, hiked), not only the verbatim query.

candidates.solves: Agents answering 'which places has X been to?' often mix future plans and aspirational reading into the list and miss implicit evidence such as photos. This skill adds a reusable rule: for past-travel questions, a location counts only with a completed event of physical presence, and searches should include activity terms that imply presence. It applies to any future enumeration of visited locations; it does not apply to questions about planned or desired destinations.

payload.name: Include event memories for hobby-duration questions
payload.description: When a question asks how long someone has been doing a hobby/practice/activity, include event memory kind in searches; do not restrict to preference/state only.
content: For duration questions about an ongoing activity (how long, for how many years, since when), run at least one search with memory_kinds including 'event' (with preference/state), because duration facts are often stored as event records.
If the initial preference/state-only search returns no duration, retry with event kind before answering 'no information'.

candidates.solves: Duration questions about a person's hobby or activity were missed because searches restricted memory_kinds to preference/state, while the duration fact was stored as an event record (e.g., 'has been practicing yoga for three years'). The reusable pattern: any 'how long has X been doing Y' query must include event memories, since duration facts for ongoing activities often live in events, not only in preference/state records.

payload.name: Search concrete follow-up action after described event
payload.description: When a question asks what activity someone did after a described event and the first search returns only the event/planning memory, run additional searches with concrete follow-up action terms before answering.
content: When a question asks what X did after an event (e.g., after reading about Y), do not treat a memory that only describes X's reading, planning, or interest around that event as evidence of the post-event activity itself.

Run additional hybrid or keyword searches combining the subject and the event's date window with concrete consequential-action vocabulary such as 'visited', 'went to', 'contacted', 'booked', 'researched', 'applied', 'agency', 'office', 'class', or 'requirements'.

If retrieved post-event memories share the event date but not its topic words, inspect them for explicit actions; continue searching until a memory states the concrete follow-up activity rather than answering from the event-description memory.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what activity someone did after a described event, the agent may over-anchor on the event's topic words and answer from a memory that describes the event or planning rather than the actual follow-up action, which is stored with different vocabulary. This skill applies to any future post-event activity question where the first retrieval returns the event/planning memory but not the concrete consequential action.

payload.name: Broaden memory kinds for recently completed activities
payload.description: When a query asks what someone recently finished, completed, read, watched, or did (e.g., just finished reading), do not restrict memory_kinds to 'event'; include 'preference' and 'state' because such facts are often stored as preferences.
content: If a question asks about a person's recently completed activity (e.g., just finished reading, recently finished, completed), set memory_kinds to include 'event', 'preference', and 'state', or omit the memory_kinds filter, since such facts are frequently stored as preference or state memories rather than events.
If an initial search restricted to 'event' returns no supporting evidence for that question, retry with broader memory_kinds (especially 'preference') before answering 'no information available'.

candidates.solves: The agent missed the answer because it restricted memory_kinds to 'event', while the supporting memory was a 'preference'. Reusable rule: for queries about recently completed activities (e.g., just finished reading, recently finished), broaden memory_kinds to include 'preference' and 'state' in addition to 'event'; applies to any future question asking what someone recently finished, read, watched, or completed.

payload.name: Event-activity terms for time-window location queries
payload.description: When a question asks where someone was or what they did in a past time window, search with travel/activity event terms and relative-time references, not only location words.
content: When a question asks where a person was or what they did in a past time window (e.g., 'the week before <date>'), do not limit searches to location words (where, whereabouts, location); also search with event/activity vocabulary such as trip, visited, traveled, went to, attended, and place names.

Include relative-time expressions (last week, last Friday, yesterday) in retrieval and resolve them to concrete dates from the session/message timestamp; treat a memory whose world_start falls within the requested window as eligible evidence even if its text expresses time relatively.
Before answering 'no information' for such a window/location question, run at least one additional search combining the subject with activity and relative-time terms.

candidates.solves: Retrieval fails when a past-window location question is searched only with location wording, missing event memories that phrase time relatively and place via activity. Adding travel/activity vocabulary and resolving relative-time references to dates transfers to any future question asking where someone was or what they did in a past period, for any person, place, or date.

payload.name: Activity-term expansion for travel-destination retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks where someone traveled/went during a time period, use activity-term query expansion and subject-only searches to retrieve location memories that do not contain the words 'travel' or the companion's role.
content: When a question asks where a person went/traveled for a period, do not limit keywords to 'travel'/'trip' or to the companion's role; the supporting memory may describe the event with activity terms such as 'retreat', 'vacation', 'getaway', 'visit', or 'attended'.

Run additional retrieval using the subject's name and the time window (e.g., name + month/year) plus activity-related terms, and also a variant without the companion's role so that a memory describing the subject alone can surface.
Before answering, verify that the candidate memory's time window overlaps the question's time period; a memory outside that window is not evidence, even if it mentions a similar location or activity.

candidates.solves: When a question asks where someone traveled or went for a time period, retrieval over-anchors on surface terms like 'travel' or the companion's role and misses memories that describe the event as an activity (e.g., retreat, vacation) in a location without those words. This skill directs query expansion with activity vocabulary and subject-only searches, and requires time-window overlap verification, so future travel-destination questions can surface the correct evidence.

payload.name: Retrieve intention-expressing memories for open-ended plan questions
payload.description: When a question asks what projects or plans a person has without naming a specific domain, use intention verbs (plans to, aims to, wants to, interested in, hopes to) in query expansions and treat memories expressing goals or interests as evidence of plans.
content: When a question asks open-endedly about someone's projects or plans (e.g., 'what is X planning?', 'what projects does X have?') without naming the domain, do not limit the search to the literal words 'project' or 'plan'. Expand the query with intention verbs and aspiration phrases such as 'plans to', 'aims to', 'wants to', 'interested in', 'hopes to', 'intends to', 'focusing on', 'developing', 'finding ways to'.

Include event memories even if their predicate is not 'project' (e.g., 'conversation', 'goal', 'interest') when the content describes future intentions or aspirations, and do not require the memory text to contain the word 'project' or 'plan'.

Before answering a 'what projects/plans' question, verify that the supporting memories express future intention or aspiration (e.g., 'plans to', 'wants to', 'aims to') rather than merely describing an ongoing/past project. If the only retrieved memories are generic 'a project' without a topic, run an additional search with the intention-verb expansions.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that retrieval for an open-ended 'what projects' question relied on literal 'project/plan' terms and stopped after one search, missing memories that convey the person's intentions through aspiration verbs (e.g., 'interested in', 'aims to', 'wants to') and conversation events. The abstraction is a reusable rule to expand with intention language and to accept such memories as evidence of plans, which transfers to any future question asking broadly about someone's planned work, goals, or initiatives.

payload.name: Resume-evidence pair for activity questions
payload.description: When a question asks what activity someone resumed, took up again, or returned to after a long time, search for past hobby/interest evidence and pair it with a recent activity event before answering.
content: If a question asks what activity someone resumed, took up again, or returned to after a long time/gap, search for preference and profile memories about past hobbies/interests (e.g., '<person> used to love <activity>', '<person> hobby') as well as event memories, before answering.

Use a resumption answer only when evidence includes both a past absence/gap statement for the activity and a later event/state of the same activity; a single same-period event is not sufficient to show a resumed activity.
If the first retrieval surfaces only unrelated same-period events, re-search with candidate activity terms and re-check preference/state memories before selecting an answer.

candidates.solves: An agent can mistake an unrelated event in the target period for the resumed activity. For questions using resume, take up again, return to, after a long time, or after a gap, require both a past absence/gap statement and a later event/state of the same activity. Does not apply to ordinary dated-activity questions without a resumption cue.

payload.name: distinguish-done-vs-interested-activities
payload.description: When a question asks what activities a person has done (completed, participated in, attended) rather than what they are interested in or plan to try, use this skill to guide retrieval and evidence judgment.
content: If the question asks what activities someone has done (e.g., 'has [subject] done', 'activities [subject] has participated in'), run multiple searches with concrete activity terms across event, preference, and plan memories before answering; do not stop after one search.

Treat only memories with explicit participation verbs ('went', 'attended', 'participated in', 'did', 'took part in') as evidence of completed activities; do not count expressions of interest, desire, or future plans ('interested in trying', 'wants to try', 'plans to') as activities done.

For each candidate activity surfaced, run a follow-up keyword search for that activity name to verify actual participation; if a memory mixes an activity the person did with one they want to try, include only the participated item.

candidates.solves: A question asked which activities a person had done, but the retrieval stopped after finding one activity and the answer included activities the person only expressed interest in trying, while missing a separate memory of an actual activity. The reusable mechanism is treating interest or intention as evidence of completion and not exhaustively searching for concrete activity names. This applies to any future question asking what activities, hobbies, or experiences someone has actually participated in or completed versus merely considered or planned.

payload.name: Include plan memories for location-period queries
payload.description: When a question asks where someone was during a date range, search plan memories and avoid strict time-window filters that exclude travel/location records.
content: When a question asks about a person's location or whereabouts during a date range, do not restrict memory_kinds to event and state; include plan memories, because past travel or visits may be recorded in plan or enriched plan memories.

Avoid using a strict time window as a hard filter for location queries; first search without time restrictions or with a broad time range, then evaluate temporal relevance from memory text and timestamps, since a plan memory's world_start may be after the queried period while its text describes an earlier trip.

Before answering a location question, require a memory that explicitly names the place; do not infer location from related events such as a team reunion or game that do not state a city, and keep searching with place-oriented terms like 'traveled to', 'visited', 'was in', or 'stayed' if explicit location evidence is missing.

candidates.solves: When a question asks where someone was during a date range, retrieval may miss the answer because location/travel information is stored in a plan or enriched plan memory whose world_start lies outside the queried window, and because search filters restricted memory kinds to event/state. This rule generalizes to any future location/whereabouts question: broaden kind and time filters so plan memories containing explicit places are considered, and avoid answering from an event that does not name a location.

payload.name: Search travel events for city-enumeration questions
payload.description: When a question asks which cities/places a person visited or mentioned visiting, even to another person, search travel/event memories and do not require the audience name or the word 'visit'.
content: If a question enumerates cities/places a person visited or mentioned visiting (e.g., 'Which US cities does X mention visiting to Y?'), run at least one hybrid search combining the person's name with travel/event terms such as 'traveled to', 'visited', 'event in', 'trip to', and 'favorite city'; do not require the audience's name or the word 'mention' to appear.

Treat event memories that locate the person in a city (upcoming games, trips, visits, 'favorite city to explore') as evidence for city visitation even when the memory does not name the audience or use the word 'visit'.
Before answering with a city list, run a supplementary search for each already-found city paired with the person's name to catch additional city memories the first query missed.

candidates.solves: Search over-anchored on the audience and the surface verb 'visiting', so a city memory stored as an event (e.g., an upcoming game in a favorite city) was never retrieved. The reusable fix is to retrieve the person's travel/event memories independently of the audience when a question enumerates cities/places visited or mentioned visiting. This applies to future 'which cities did X visit/mention to Y' questions where location evidence may live in event memories without the audience's name.

payload.name: SearchProfileKindsForMembershipQueries
payload.description: When a question asks what classes, courses, groups, workshops, or organizations a person has joined, attended, or participates in, include profile and state memory kinds, not only event/plan.
content: When answering what classes, courses, groups, workshops, or memberships a person has joined/attends/participates in, do not restrict memory_kinds to event and plan; also search profile, state, and preference kinds because ongoing affiliations are often stored there.

Run at least one complementary search using membership phrasing such as 'is a member of', 'joined', 'participates in', or 'signed up for' without a restrictive memory-kind filter, then aggregate all named classes/groups from every retrieved memory before answering.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure: the agent answered a question about joined classes/groups using only event/plan memory kinds and missed a profile memory recording an ongoing group membership. Sustained memberships, affiliations, and enrolled courses are frequently stored as profile/state facts rather than one-off events, so memory-kind restrictions hide them. This rule applies to any future question asking what classes, courses, groups, workshops, or organizations a person has joined, attended, or participates in.

payload.name: Search descriptive adjectives for habitual activity places
payload.description: When a question asks what type of place a person regularly meditates, relaxes, or practices wellness activities, and first results show only named retreats or generic memories.
content: Run an additional search combining the person's name, the activity, and descriptive location adjectives like tranquil, quiet, peaceful, nearby, or favorite.
Prefer a current habitual setting memory over a past named destination when the question implies recurring practice; use memory kind and world_start/world_end to distinguish.
Do not choose the most explicit place name; require a memory connecting the person, the activity, and a place descriptor.

candidates.solves: A literal activity+place search missed a memory describing the habitual spot as 'nearby tranquil spot' and selected a one-time retreat instead. This happens when a question asks for a regular activity's location and the correct memory uses descriptive adjectives rather than a place noun. The rule applies to wellness/leisure activities with one-time destination distractors.

payload.name: Enumerate places visited in a specific time window
payload.description: When a question asks which places (or all places) a person visited during a specific month or period, gather every candidate location memory, verify timestamps, and expand searches with discovered place and activity terms before answering.
content: When a question asks which places a person visited in a specific time window, treat it as an enumeration task: keep searching until follow-up queries stop surfacing new candidate place memories, and do not answer from the first retrieved location alone.

For each retrieved travel/activity memory, extract its named places and activity descriptors (e.g., road trip, skiing, hiking) and use those as additional query terms in later searches instead of reusing the original query or the first place name.

Before counting a candidate place, verify its memory world_start/world_end falls within the requested period; exclude any candidate whose timestamp is outside the window even if it is the only or highest-scoring result.
When multiple candidates have in-period evidence, include all distinct places in the answer rather than selecting a single one.

candidates.solves: Future questions that ask which places (including 'which places...', 'all places...') a person visited during a specific month or period. The diagnosed cause is that the agent anchored on the first retrieved location, used an out-of-window memory as evidence, and missed other in-window places because follow-up searches reused the original query rather than terms mined from retrieved memories. The rule transfers to any location enumeration question with a temporal constraint; it does not apply to open-ended location questions without a time window.

payload.name: Search concrete project names for category questions
payload.description: When a question asks what kind(s) or type(s) of projects, items, or work someone has done, search using concrete object/domain terms and enumerate distinct named projects before answering.
content: When a question asks what kind(s) or type(s) of projects, items, or work a person has done, treat one generic query as insufficient; it can return vague 'project' memories instead of concrete named projects.

Run at least one additional hybrid or keyword search using concrete object nouns or domain-specific project terms (not only the generic category label), with memory_kinds ['event','plan'] before answering.
Enumerate distinct named projects from all retrieved event/plan memories; include a specific named project even if its memory was not the top-ranked hit.

candidates.solves: A category question such as 'what kind of engineering projects has this person worked on?' often receives one generic search, so vague 'project' memories crowd out concrete named projects. The failure is a retrieval rule gap: category-enumeration questions need object-level searches and enumeration of distinct named memories. The rule applies to any question asking kinds/types of projects, creative work, or owned items, but not to questions about a single project or a numeric count.

payload.name: Physical-transformation query vocabulary expansion
payload.description: When a question asks about a person's physical transformation or appearance change in a date range, and initial retrieval returns no direct evidence, use concrete appearance-change terms and re-search before answering.
content: When a question asks what physical transformation or appearance change someone underwent in a time period, do not rely only on abstract phrases like 'physical transformation' or 'appearance change'; run additional searches using concrete change verbs and nouns (dyed, colored, hair, tattoo, piercing, shaved, cut, styled, gained/lost weight, glasses).

Treat an appearance-change memory as one whose text may not contain the abstract category label or exact date-range wording; after an initial search returns only unrelated events, issue another search combining the subject, concrete appearance-change vocabulary, and the target time window (or world_start filter) before concluding no information.

Do not answer 'No information available' after a single top-k retrieval for a physical-change question; require at least one expanded concrete-term search and inspect event memories with world_start inside the target period as potential evidence.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that a query built only from the abstract category term missed the concrete stored event, and the agent stopped after one unfruitful search. The reusable mechanism is abstract-question vocabulary mismatch for appearance-change events, which applies whenever a future question asks what physical/appearance change a person underwent in a dated window. The rule forces concrete-term expansion and at least one additional search before answering no-information.

payload.name: EnumerateAdditionalItemsViaCategorySearches
payload.description: When answering enumeration questions about read/watched/played/consumed items, after an initial search returns some items, run additional searches for generic category descriptions before finalizing.
content: If the question asks for a list or enumeration of items a person has read, watched, played, or consumed, do not finalize the answer after one search even if it returns some concrete items.

Run additional hybrid or keyword searches pairing the activity with generic category descriptors likely present in memories (e.g., 'non-fiction', 'series', 'fantasy', 'personal development', 'mystery') and inspect both event and preference memories for items described by category.
Aggregate all distinct named or clearly described items from all searches before composing the answer; if only one search was performed, treat the list as potentially incomplete.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for an enumeration of items a person has read/watched/played/consumed, an initial search may return some named items yet miss memories that describe additional items by category. The diagnosed failure was stopping after one retrieval and omitting category-described books. Applies to any future list/enumeration query where relevant memories may describe items generically; run supplementary searches before answering.

payload.name: Ensure per-person item evidence for activity-enhancement questions
payload.description: When a question asks what ways, methods, or items multiple people use to enhance or improve an activity, verify each named person has concrete item evidence and run targeted per-person preference/event searches if one has only generic activity memories.
content: When the question asks what ways or items people use to enhance/improve an activity, treat it as requiring concrete enhancers for each named person, not merely the activity itself.

After retrieval, map evidence to each named person. If a person has only generic activity memories, run a supplementary hybrid search with that person's name, the activity, and common enhancement-item terms (e.g., scents, music, equipment, atmosphere, 'prefers', 'purchased'), including preference and event memory kinds.
Do not answer until every named person either has a concrete enhancement item in evidence or a targeted per-person search has been attempted.

candidates.solves: The failure occurred because a multi-person 'how do they enhance X' question was answered from generic activity memories, missing one person's concrete enhancement items stored in preference/event memories. The reusable rule is to verify per-person evidence of concrete enhancers and run targeted per-person item searches before answering. It applies to future questions asking what ways/methods/items multiple people use to enhance or improve an activity; it does not apply to questions seeking only general activities without specific enhancement items.

payload.name: EnumerateAllItemsForListQuestions
payload.description: When a user asks for a list of items (e.g., classes, courses, activities, hobbies) that a person took, attended, or is involved in, do not answer after finding one relevant memory; search multiple phrasings and memory kinds and aggregate all distinct items.
content: When a question asks for a list of items (e.g., 'what are the classes/courses/activities/hobbies'), treat it as an enumeration request: do not stop after the first supporting memory or after a single search.

Run multiple searches with varied phrasings and synonyms (e.g., class, course, workshop, training, seminar, activity) and include relevant memory kinds such as 'event', 'profile', and 'state'; for enrollments or sign-ups, include 'event' memories with future world_start if the query also covers planned or registered items.

Before answering, gather all distinct items from the combined retrieved set; if the retrieved set lacks enough distinct items or the question implies multiple, issue additional searches before finalizing.

candidates.solves: When a question asks to enumerate a person's items (e.g., classes taken, courses attended, activities, hobbies), the diagnosed failure was answering from the first retrieved memory only, missing other supported items. The reusable mechanism is that plural-list questions require multiple synonym searches and cross-kind evidence aggregation before answering. This applies to any future list-eliciting query about a person's activities, courses, or possessions, but not to questions seeking a single fact or a yes/no confirmation.

payload.name: Search collection-specific vocabulary for collection enumeration
payload.description: Use when a question asks what items a person collects or what their collection includes; run supplementary searches using collection terms and concrete category items.
content: If a question asks what items a person collects or what their collection includes, do not answer from one generic search like 'items <person> collects'. Run additional hybrid searches with collection-specific phrasings: '<person> collection', '<person> collects', '<person> likes to collect', and '<person> enjoys collecting'.

Before finalizing, generate concrete collectible category terms from the person's interests and run at least one search combining those terms with the person's name; preference memories may mention an item only as an enjoyment/interest (e.g., 'enjoys X', 'interested in X') without using the word 'collect'.
When gathering candidates, include distinct items named in preference memories as collection evidence even if the memory does not explicitly say the person collects them.

candidates.solves: Questions enumerating a person's collected items often fail with one generic 'items <person> collects' query because preference memories describe collections indirectly (e.g., 'collection of sneakers', 'enjoys fantasy movies'). This skill adds collection-specific query variants and category-term searches so future questions retrieve all indirectly stated collectibles. Applies to 'what does X collect' questions, not to non-collection enumerations like counts of owned items.
